t: I Told You So Is Leadership Profanity
q: That’s because they know very few leadership phrases invoke as much distaste, disgust, and defensiveness as those four simple words.
Telling others that you knew all along that they would fail or misstep is akin to a slap in the face.
Leaders who use the expression diminish the trust and support necessary for others to admit a mistake or take accountability in the future.
But it is the leader who doesn’t realize they are saying it that creates the most harm.
I told you so” is leadership profanity. Good leaders don’t swear at people when they make an avoidable mistake.

t: AI Makes Student Knowledge MORE Important, Not Less
q: AI is like a souped up calculator — its usefulness is multiplied by the intelligence of its user, and that intelligence is built on a mountain of knowledge.

when students constantly Google (or ChatGPT) information instead of learning it, they never make the shift from conscious recall to automatic expertise. They stay stuck in the slow, effortful mode of thinking because they never build the internal knowledge structures that make advanced thinking possible.

Oakley’s team found that students who rely too heavily on AI for writing and problem-solving show weaker brain connectivity in regions linked to focus and memory. They develop what researchers call “metacognitive laziness” — they let the tool do the thinking instead of building their own cognitive muscles.

guess what kinds of students benefit most from AI? Those who already have strong foundational knowledge. They can evaluate AI output, ask better questions, and integrate suggestions meaningfully. Students without that foundation just accept whatever the AI produces.
memorization isn’t the enemy of critical thinking — it’s the foundation.

Knowledge is what allows us to make sense of all that external information, to ask the right questions, and to think clearly about complex problems. It gives us access to the cosmos and the breadth of human experience.

t: The Impact of Strong Interpersonal Connections in the Workplace
q: According to a recent Gallup study, team members who have friends in the workplace are seven times more likely to be highly engaged at their jobs.
Good leaders don’t presume close working relationships will always happen organically.
Rather than sponsor a solitary team member to engage in a professional development program or experience outside of the organization, they underwrite team members to attend as dyads or triads.
When team members travel, dine, and attend sessions together over an extended period of time, they often form closer ties.
Good leaders want close relationships between colleagues to form naturally, but know sometimes they need a little push.

t: Who Is the Right Person to Make the Decision
q: The “right” person usually makes a world of difference. So, what goes into making this meta-decision (the decision about who decides) is worth weighing seriously.
But those with an in-depth working knowledge of the issues often overplay their expertise and allow their pre-existing biases to influence the decision process and outcome.
More important than expertise or track record, good leaders depend on others who have the bandwidth to spend the necessary time to reach a quality outcome.
Without saying so, they often select a decision-maker they believe is already close to where they think the decision should land.
When it comes to delegating important decisions, good leaders put a thumb on the scale.

t: Scaling Learning Interventions: A Case Study in Interleaved Math Practice https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3698205.3729554 math-practice/
q: The authors note that despite strong evidence for its effectiveness, interleaved practice is rarely incorporated into math curricula, highlighting a disconnect between learning research and educational application.

Implementing interleaved practice is not straightforward. Despite strong evidence that it can improve math learning, blocked practice predominates existing math curricula, meaning teachers often lack readily available interleaved materials.
Communicating learning principles like interleaving to teachers is necessary but not sufficient for them to utilize the research in practice.
Teachers face a flood of contextual challenges when attempting to modify assignments for interleaving.
There is a critical need for feasible, concrete classroom materials and practical implementation models that reduce the burden on teachers and fit within class constraints.

Initial findings from our first cohort indicated that students who received interleaved practice scored, on average, higher than students who received blocked practice on both a) a researcher developed assessment, and b) externally developed assessments on ratios and proportions and number systems, but none of these differences were statistically significant

t: Lead With Competence and Belonging Will Follow
q: There’s a common misconception amongst us teachers about how to develop Belonging in the classroom, and it’s this: at the start of the school year, you need to budget lots of time for things like icebreakers, get-to-know-you activities, and team-building exercises.

When you try to help your students develop a sense of Belonging to a class that hasn’t even started yet (because instead of beginning to teach the class, you’re focusing on cultivating belonging), you’re creating an unnatural thing. Instead, you want to create something worth belonging TO.
Rather than lots of icebreakers and get-to-know-yous, create enjoyable and productive learning experiences.
Who WOULDN’T want to believe they belong in a class led by a credible educator? Who WOULDN’T want to believe they belong in a class where the work is valuable?
The human heart is DRAWN to excellence, to value, to competence, to growth.

t: Enhancing Final Exam Performance Through Retrieval Practice: Evidence From a Diverse College Sample https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/00986283251352475
q: Retrieval practice improved overall exam scores across various question types, including rephrased and applied concepts, and also reduced perceived exam difficulty and anxiety among students.
This learning strategy is simple to implement and requires minimal preparation.
Instructors should encourage retrieval practice both in class and for independent study, especially when students are preparing for formal assessments.
Retrieval practice improves student performance on final exams, benefiting not just factual questions, but also applied and even unrelated questions.
Students who engage in retrieval practice report less worry or anxiety about their exam grade and perceive the exam as less difficult.
This study replicated and extended past findings by showing that a brief retrieval practice activity benefits diverse learners in the classroom.

t: Consider Your Feedback Density
q: The impact of feedback is most influenced by three critical qualities: how good it is, how frequent it is, and how dense it is.
Feedback density refers to the sheer quantity of commentary offered during critical times of development, such as practice and rehearsal.
In both athletics and in the workplace, dense positive feedback is uplifting and promotes confidence.
In contrast, critical or negative feedback that is highly dense overwhelms people. It is typically too much to process and only leaves a negative feeling.
If you’re going to be dense, make it positive. Otherwise, offer a small set of critical points, explain those points succinctly, and move on.

t: Leaders Who Act as Jupiter
q: Jupiter’s magnetic field is the strongest in the solar system, over 20,000 times stronger than Earth’s.
They view their most important function as liberating team members from outside distractions and threats to their productivity.
Instead, they operate as if they are at the center of their team, with everything revolving around them.
Strong leaders take on the brunt of external criticism and organizational pressures so their teams can focus on the work that matters.
The best leaders don't act like the Sun, operating like they are the center spoke of all team activity. They act like Jupiter.

t: The Practice of Giving Advance Notice for Workforce Reductions
q: As part of this cost-cutting planning process, how to communicate a reduction in headcount to both internal team members and external stakeholders is hugely consequential.
What is so confusing is why so many organizations announce RIFs through the media, sometimes even before team members learn of the impending changes.
By releasing the information to the media themselves, leaders convince themselves that they can control the narrative.
When team members are blindsided by unexpected news of reductions, they naturally feel betrayed, disrespected, and disenfranchised.
Good leaders don’t make that call because they value people more than they value short-term gain.

t: Why Establishing Classroom Management Is Easier In August
q: The window opens the moment the bell rings on day one and closes less than three weeks later.
Therefore, they’re at their most open, most attentive, and most willing to follow a real-deal leader.
Otherwise, bad behaviors, bad habits, and bad attitudes will grow like autumn azaleas.

The reason is confidence, or lack thereof. The potential for aggressive pushback from students, and even more brazen misbehavior, is so great that they fear taking the stand they should have taken the first day of school.
You have the best opportunity you’re ever going to get to have the teaching experience you really want.

t: Creating an Appetite for Feedback
q: Leaders who want team members to seek feedback need to do three things: ask for feedback, act on it, and tell the giver when it has had an impact.
Try asking a better question than “How did I do?” — a phrase that can come across as fishing for a compliment.
Leaders show others that their feedback is valuable when they act on it.
Good leaders go a step further and describe how important the suggestion was.
As a rule, team members won’t seek feedback from a leader until they have earned it. Be the kind of leader who makes others hungry for input.

t: Should You Ask Team Members to Read Before Discussions
q: Former Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos detested slide deck presentations because they too often allowed for a superficial overview and discussion of the issues involved in a critical project or decision.
At the start of meetings, attendees spend about 30 minutes in silence reading the memo, creating a deep understanding of the issues.
Unlike similar organizations with critical decisions to make, leaders at Amazon spend between one and four hours writing and reading every day.
Current CEO Andy Jassy credits this writing process with teaching him how to thoroughly consider ideas and to present them logically for others.
Perhaps attempting the six-page memo and silent reading on one critical issue would prove a valuable experiment.

t: First Days of School Writing Prompts
q: asking students what they did over summer break can put students with sub-optimal summer vacations into a bad spot right out of the gate.
What is a goal you’ve set for yourself this school year? Gets students defining success right out of the gate (Strategy #9 in The Will to Learn).

It signals that in this class we will do the hard and good work of writing. It is very important to get into the actual work of learning as quickly as possible in the school year. Writing on Day One sends a strong message.

It signals that you are a teacher who cares to hear from your students. This helps with your Credibility. It also helps with Belonging, as any time you get students writing about their own experience or the things they value, you’re tapping into the demonstrated power of Values Affirmation interventions.
Give yourself permission to read a few per class period per day in the first month of school and to connect with the students once you’ve read them.

t: Learn to Speak in Headlines
q: The more senior the audience, the more important it is to speak in headlines.
What senior audiences want is the lay of the land, not a topographical map.
Starting with strategic headlines before diving into any topic or issue is how leaders talk to leaders.
Experts love to overwhelm people with the facts and details they know because it displays their deep understanding and knowledge.
People don’t read the copy before they read the headline for a simple reason: They have no idea why the copy matters without a summarizing statement.

t: Why Asking a Lot From Team Members Makes Them More Committed
q: Leaders with high standards and expectations, and who are relationally supportive of team members, amplify motivation, confidence, and commitment in those who follow them.
Psychologists call this the Pygmalion Effect after the Greek myth of a sculptor whose belief in the beauty of his statue brought it to life.
Many coaches are cautious about asking too much from players because they fear the players might pick up and go elsewhere. But the best college coaches do the opposite.
Leaders who are not college athletic coaches don’t normally think of it this way, but they have always operated in an open transfer portal.
The answer to this challenge is not to lower expectations and demands but to raise them.

t: Value via Purpose Tapping into a Nuclear Power Source of Student Motivation https://davestuartjr.com/value-via-purpose-tapping-into-a-nuclear-power-source-of-student-motivation
q: Purpose is a stable and generalized intention to accomplish something that is at the same time meaningful to the self and consequential to the world beyond the self.
Unmoored by a sense of purpose, they drift, often experiencing higher rates of anxiety, depression, and disengagement.
When students can connect their learning to a larger purpose, they stop asking, “When will I ever use this?
Damon urges teachers to tell students why we’re teachers. One of the best predictors of the development of purpose in young people is the presence of what he calls purpose exemplars in their lives.

Mini-sermons aren’t optional in today’s classrooms; they are essential to Value cultivation in general, and they help a lot with purpose development when we speak into the purpose of learning math or science or whatever we’re teaching.
When we cultivate the will to learn, we’re not just improving test scores. We’re helping young people discover what they’re here for.

t: Research Bite #34: Noise, Cognitive Function, and Worker Productivity
q: This document explores the impact of noise on worker productivity in a real-world setting.
Through experiments with textile workers, it demonstrates that increased noise levels reduce output, suggesting that noise significantly impairs cognitive function, which is crucial for such tasks.

Noise can impair cognitive functions, such as attention and working memory, which are crucial for task management and performance, and individuals (like the workers in this study) may not be aware of how significantly noise affects their performance
Excessive noise can significantly impair students' cognitive functions, such as attention and working memory, which are crucial for learning and academic success.
The research found that even a 10 dB increase in noise (equivalent to moving from a dishwasher to a vacuum cleaner's sound) reduces performance.
This cautions against the ability of workers to appropriately adapt to the impacts of noise and suggests dealing with environmental cognitive impediments may require policy intervention

t: Reciprocity and the Domino Effect of Kindness
q: Participants who received the unsolicited gift of a Coke bought twice as many raffle tickets as those who did not receive anything from Joe.
People repaid the unexpected small favor by helping Joe, even when their opinion of him was neutral or negative.
Over time, unexpected acts of help, support, and recognition throughout the team create a domino effect of proactive generosity.
Central to this transformation is consistency and genuineness. The leader and team members must sustain their generosity without expecting anything in return.
Reciprocity usually occurs with each act of a leader’s kindness, but does not become pervasive across the team until other team members join in without being asked.

t: Leaders Obsessed With Excellence Can Become Monsters
q: Ordinarily normal people who become obsessed with creating excellence often become monsters along the way.
Their relentless pursuit of excellence allows them to justify whatever actions they deem necessary to accomplish it with the highest quality.
The team becomes a revolving door for talent. From the outside, the passion and dedication can appear alluring to some, but once on the inside, most retreat.
When one well-known leader was named by a magazine as the second meanest boss in a city, they complained about not being first.
The pursuit of excellence is a virtuous endeavor. But when it becomes an obsession, it can turn angels into demons.

t: The Signs of Overcollaboration
q: In these workplaces, the problem is not that team members communicate too little with each other but that they engage too much.
Overcollaboration is a serious issue and manifests itself in slow and ineffective decision-making and an endless stream of unproductive meetings.
Group chats to coordinate efforts and share knowledge become more important than the work itself.
This collaboration overload reduces productivity and job satisfaction, leading to mental exhaustion and apathy.
Of course, if your instinct is to involve too many people in such a decision, it likely will never see the light of day. That is strong evidence that you truly have an overcollaboration problem.

t: When Asked About a Colleague, Speak as if They Were in the Room
q: The best rule of thumb is to only speak about others as if they were in the room with you.
When people are highly critical of a colleague, they are typically more direct, and they speak more descriptively than they usually do.
Staying respectful is aided when leaders couch criticisms as questions or concerns, rather than as assertions or statements of fact.
Once a leader goes too far in their criticisms of a colleague who isn’t present, they undermine the trust they need to lead.
Those present wonder if the leader is equally condemning of them when they are not in the room. Trust erodes from all sides.

t: What I've Learned from Direct Instruction
q: I've learned a lot from Direct Instruction but I still have no desire to become a Direct Instruction teacher. DI doesn't provide much variety in how students participate -- it's mostly choral response, cold calling, and written work.
I say, "think in your head, what is 50% of 12?" I pause and let students think. Then I raise my hand above my head, say, "Ready, go", as I say go I bring my hand down, and students say the answer.
Now I use choral response in most lessons. It's quick -- often 2-4 minutes of total time in a lesson.
To put a number on it, a typical Direct Instruction lesson spends about 80-90% of the time practicing and reviewing ideas that have been introduced previously.
The more I do this, the more little skills I find to teach before we start a unit, and the smoother that unit goes.
My opinion is that far too many teachers don't know anything about Direct Instruction, and they would have a lot to learn if they were open to it.

t: The Most Important Thing On The First Day Of School -school/
q: When your students leave for home after the first day of school, they must already love being in your class.
Because, when your students feel lucky that you’re their teacher, they’ll want to listen to you, behave for you, and please you.
This is what you want on the first day. To leave your students happily shaken, with a buzzing in their ears and a slow-fading glow from a classroom experience they never expected.
Instead, have fun and be friendly and pleasant from the very first minute.
Make it exceptional and enjoyable. Put yourself in their shoes. Ease their fears. Make them smile.

t: 6 Habits That Quietly Harm Your Career, And How to Shift Them -to-shift-them/
q: Throughout my career, I've observed that most professional derailments don't come from lack of talent, they come from habits. Often unconscious, they chip away at our growth slowly, like water eroding rock.
Silence may feel like safety, but avoidance breeds resentment. Whether it's a colleague who crossed a line, or a student who needs honest feedback, evading tough talks only magnifies issues.
Perfectionism is often celebrated, but in truth, it's fear in a polished coat. It tells us not to start unless it's flawless, and not to finish if it isn't.
In our drive to please, many of us say yes far too often, to extra tasks, favours, or responsibilities that don't align with our goals.
The fear of being "too much" can lead us to become too quiet. Yet, sharing our achievements is not arrogance, it's awareness.
Careers are not built in giant leaps but in daily choices. As with teaching and research, the goal isn't perfection, it's progress.

t: 3-Read Friday #80: Lethal Mutations, Career Habits, and Direct Instruction
q: Hali examines how potentially effective principles from research have been misapplied in schools -- such as interleaving, growth mindset, and retrieval practice -- and what schools can do about it.
Nimish examines six habits he has seen hold back himself or his colleagues, and suggests strategies to overcome them. How many can you relate to?
Dylan took a deep dive into the Direct Instruction world, concluded that it was not for him, but found three principles that he has taken forward into his teaching. A great read!
Here are three blog posts that I found interesting this week.
6 Habits That Quietly Harm Your Career, And How to Shift Them by Nimish Lad.

t: Are You an Agile Learner
q: The ability to learn quickly from experiences and apply that learning to new, unfamiliar situations suggests someone who has learning agility.
Unlike most people, who form a strong impression of others and then collect data to confirm that view, agile learners allow their opinions of others to change over time.
Agile learners aren't stuck or blinded by what has already been proposed to tackle an issue, but can easily generate other approaches or possibilities to expand the discussion.
Unlike most of their peers, agile learners are actually charged up by the prospect of change.
Given the importance of learning agility for organizations to thrive amid rapid and unpredictable change, you need to select and develop more team members who possess this crucial quality.

t: Beyond a Recognition of Results
q: Leaders who only recognize and reward outcomes and results miss a critical link affecting so many of the qualities they want from their team members.
Performers at all skill levels want to know that their under-the-radar investments to achieve success are prized as highly as the success itself.

They go out of their way to recognize and acknowledge, both publicly and privately, the underlying sacrifices, qualities, and energies that help to produce results, even when the outcomes are disappointing.
Recognizing or praising effort, especially with children, is known as a key motivator for future undertakings, but it is less impactful with adults.
Best of all, such recognition is absolutely free, yet worth a fortune to team success.

t: This Is the Year of Value
q: But parents don't send their children to school just to have relationships. They send them to school to learn things — to grow toward mastery.

So what happens when a culture obsessed with utility and relevance gets flooded with magical algorithmic engagement machines (smartphones) in the 2010s and sophisticated AI tools in the 2020s? The Value of school plummets.

It is my view that in this coming school year and the few that follow, schools that double down on Value cultivation will separate themselves from schools that do not. Some of these schools will lean heavily on AI; others will forbid its use completely.
Value cultivation is hard, for sure. Especially with the AI-related changes to culture and work and school that none of us opted-in for.
Value cultivation has always been an important skill set with great rewards. The more we help our students value the work of learning, the more they'll be drawn to do that work with care.

Schools have always struggled to help students genuinely believe that learning is good. In ultra-pragmatic and individualistic cultures like the United States, schools tend to heavily rely on the Value avenues of utility and relevance.

t: How Clean Is Your Car
q: A NASCAR crew chief’s success relies heavily on the capabilities and performance of their team.
He doesn’t care what kind of car they drive (old, new, flashy, expensive, or modified). He only wants to know one thing—do they take care of it?
If the car isn’t clean and well-maintained, Knaus turns the candidate down. He figures if you don’t take care of your stuff, you aren’t going to take good care of his.

For instance, what if you walked into a prospective candidate’s workspace and saw stacks of papers, boxes, and trash? Would the assumption that they were disorganized and likely to have cluttered thinking be fair and important?
Others may argue that they are biased in their judgments over their inferences, but almost every good judge of talent relies on some.

t: The Key Discipline for Following Up
q: Without effective follow-up, the necessary momentum needed to work toward completion of an initiative often sputters and results in a disappointing outcome.
Everyone knows the essential ingredients of great follow-up: gathering more information, checking on progress, providing additional support, repeating a previous action.
The key to follow-up is to define what further actions are necessary to ensure progress before completing the last step.
Examine the task list of a highly productive leader or team member, and you will see as many follow-up actions as you do new responsibilities to be completed.
Great follow-up doesn’t just communicate excellence. It creates it.

t: Research Bite #33: Is Covert Retrieval an Effective Learning Strategy?
q: This academic meta-analysis investigates the effectiveness of covert retrieval, recalling information mentally, as a learning strategy compared to overt retrieval, which involves physically producing a response.

Analyzing data from numerous studies, the research finds that covert retrieval offers a small but significant benefit for learning, especially for complex materials and long-term retention, and when corrective feedback is provided.

While retrieval practice is a powerful learning tool overall, overt retrieval is generally more effective than covert retrieval for enhancing student learning, and educators should prioritize using methods that require students to actively produce responses
Answer monitoring, where students passively judge another's answer, is not effective.
Teachers should exercise caution due to the modest overall learning benefits of covert retrieval (g = 0.23).
While covert retrieval can enhance learning of educationally relevant materials and consolidate long-term retention, it is generally less effective than overt retrieval

t: How To Infuriate A Concerned Parent
q: The biggest mistake you can make is to hear them out. The more they can provide proof of their concerns, the more dangerous it is for you.
You never want to do this. Protect your ego at all costs. Besides, you always know better.
This strategy is the chef’s kiss. It will shut them down and burn their insides out.
If you see even a hint of yourself in any of the seven steps, I want you to know that parents aren’t your enemy and there are honest guidelines you can follow.
To be clear, of course I’m not recommending that you anger parents. The article is a literary device intended to make a strong point.

t: Three Words Aren't Enough: Rethinking Motivation
q: For a few decades now, Richard Deci and Edward Ryan have developed self-determination theory: a theory of academic motivation that gets LOTS of love.
We should start by admitting that LOTS of people who talk about self-determination theory don't get past these headlines.
On the one hand, that advice could certainly foster a sense of relatedness in the classroom... At the same time, offering hints might lessen another student's sense of autonomy.
Yes, you will hear "autonomy! relatedness!! competence!!!" offered as a formula to enhance student motivation. But I don't think this formula -- or ANY formula -- works simply as a formula.
On the other hand, students who lack appropriate prior knowledge could be overwhelmed and demotivated by all that time to work alone.
In other words: if I worry that my students lack motivation, I shouldn't simply look at that list and pick one that sounds uplifting and research-y.

t: Teaching the Limited Capacity Brain: A Visual Guide and Model nd-model/
q: It is hopefully not too controversial a statement to say that attention and working memory are limited in capacity (and in their duration too, for that matter).
The important thing to take from all this though is that attention is a complete bottleneck to higher order processing, the gateway to complex cognition.
Unfortunately, increasing capacity (i.e. training) doesn't really seem to work for either attention or working memory.
This gives us our first key teaching message. That we need to do out best to reduce distractions in the classroom wherever possible.
Even more importantly in terms of overcoming capacity limitations, information which is meaningfully connected in long term memory can be recalled into working memory as a single 'chunk'.
This means that as teachers we need to ideally provide students with retrieval opportunities (which will strengthen retrieval strength) in advance of the students needing it.

t: Managing the Anxious Attachment Style
q: A common issue on teams is one or more members who possess an anxious attachment style and display a deep insecurity about how others perceive them.
These team members have a constant need for approval and reassurance, seek feedback but interpret constructive criticism as a personal rejection.
An anxious attachment style is rarely pacified through increased attention.
This sounds cruel, but it actually creates structure for the afflicted party to find their own discipline about seeking unnecessary validation.
The more a leader treats this anxious attachment style team member in the same way they do others, the sooner everyone can establish whether this arrangement can work long-term.

t: Correct Answers But No Learning
q: When I asked her how she was doing so well in making the words and to talk me through her strategy, she said: "You just match the colours, Dad.

The surface features of the task (colour-matching) are more salient than the underlying cognitive goal (phoneme blending). She completed the task correctly, but without actually practising the skill it was supposed to develop.
My daughter experienced what Robert Bjork call "illusions of comprehension and competence": the misleading sense that she had mastered the skill when she had merely found a workaround.

This is why we should be deeply sceptical of "engagement" as a metric for educational effectiveness. A child who is busily occupied, enthusiastically participating, and producing correct responses may be learning nothing of value.
Learning doesn't always happen when the student completes a task. It's what happens when the task causes the student to think. Instructional design is not neutral, it always teaches something.

t: 3-Read Friday #79: Motivation, Working Memory, and Correct Answers Without Learning
q: I love Andrew's research deep-dives. Here, he explores Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory, delving beyond the headlines to consider what this concept looks like in the classroom.
A super clear overview of the limitations of our brains in terms of attention and working memory capacity.
The illustrations are especially useful and could be shared with students to help them better understand how they learn.
Gosh, Carl is banging out some good blog posts at the moment. This one reflects on an experience he had watching his daughter complete a card sort.
Here are three blog posts that I found interesting this week.

t: Tour de France The Ultimate Display of Teamwork
q: What isn’t known, except to avid cycling fans, is how the race is the embodiment of teamwork.
They push aside their own ambition and desire for individual performance and focus exclusively on protecting the leader from race risks and a loss of energy.
This allows the leader to conserve up to 40 percent more energy compared to riding alone.
The Tour de France highlights individual champions, but victory is only possible when each team rider plays a specific role to promote the leader.

When everyone on a team aligns around a unified purpose, understands their role in propelling the team toward success, and stands ready to sacrifice their personal agendas for the good of the team, great results happen.

t: If a Leader Had Only One Question They Could Ask
q: But if a leader had only one question they could ask, the most powerful inquiry is “What do you think?
When a leader asks for input, it shows they respect the other party’s knowledge and perspective.
Leaders who ask for a view signal that they don’t have all the answers and have yet to land on a conclusion. This openness fosters trust.
By asking this question of those with far less expertise, experience, and skillfulness, leaders show a humility that builds trust within a team.
Of the many questions a leader might ask, “What do you think?” carries the most weight.

t: Dialogue: The heartbeat of instructional coaching
q: A 2018 meta-analysis of 60 studies showed that instructional coaching has large positive effects on both instructional practice and student achievement: The quality of teachers' instruction improves by as much as - or more than - the difference in effectiveness between a novice and a teacher with five to 10 years of experience.

One of the biggest lethal mutations I see of this model is that it becomes a checklist to be worked through as quickly as possible, which inevitably means that coaches/mentors just talk at their coachee/mentee for 15 minutes.
Mental models are internal representations that guide how individuals interpret and respond to situations. Through dialogue, coaches help teachers make their implicit reasoning explicit.

Lofthouse and Hall introduced the idea of the coaching dialogic space - a professional environment characterised by trust, openness and curiosity. Within this space, teachers can test ideas, process emotions and take professional risks.
So the next time we think about improving teaching, let's start with a conversation, because when we talk, we think. When we think better, we teach better.

t: The Fine Line Between High Engagement and Micromanagement
q: Micromanagers monitor even low-priority tasks and assignments and often give frequent feedback about what they believe are the right choices for executing them.
When micromanaged, team members feel undervalued, underappreciated, and suspect in their problem-solving abilities.
Good leaders keep their eyes on and their hands off everything that is going on in the team.
They check in on occasion with two questions: What should I know? And what can I do to help?
Eyes on, Hands off,” unless the project needs to be saved. Then it’s “Hands on” all the way.

t: Avoiding lethal mutations – How schools can keep research alive and effective
q: This phenomenon is known as the lethal mutation, a term originally coined by Ed Haertel and highlighted in the work of Brown and Campione. It describes how research-based strategies can lose their potency when oversimplified, misunderstood or applied without context.
Unlike edu-myths - which are just wrong from the start - lethal mutations are more dangerous because they begin with good intentions and sound research.
It's a bit like that famous Morecambe and Wise sketch - teachers are playing the right notes, but they're in the wrong order.

While 100% of surveyed teachers reported using retrieval practice regularly, the most common format was short-answer quizzes (used by 85%). More effective or diverse formats like matching or fill-in-the-blank were rarely used.
Lethal mutations don't happen because teachers are careless. They happen when schools rush to adopt ideas without creating the conditions for deep understanding and professional dialogue.

t: Research Bite #32: Cognitive Load Theory: Emerging Trends and Innovations
q: This review finds that CLT research predominantly employs experimental or intervention designs (14 out of 16 reviewed articles).
The paper concludes that CLT research is more scientifically rigorous in its methodology, justifying the recommendations for practice derived from these studies.
Tablet-based AR was found to reduce ECL for university students with particularly low spatial abilities.
Teachers would be well advised to focus on raising students' interest, especially when students are expected to process tasks or problems that are very easy for them.

Recommendations for practice derived from CLT research, particularly from experimental methods, are based on solid ground, giving teachers specific guidance on when and how to implement strategies and approaches.
Overall, this Special Issue reaffirms the ongoing relevance of cognitive load theory in modern learning contexts.

t: Have You Ever Met Someone Who Is Very Funny and Isnt Smart
q: As a shortcut to assessing whether someone has the brainpower to tackle a job or position, it is a treasure.
Humor and wit are strong indicators of cognitive and emotional intelligence. It takes abstract reasoning, creativity, and social awareness to be exceptionally funny.
If you want to use humor as a shortcut to intelligence, the better tack is to give people the opportunity to be funny and see how they do.
You wake up and discover you are invisible, but only to co-workers. What do you do with this superpower?
Give people an opening, and funny people will say something comical or amusing.

t: Asking Team Members to Carry on the Legacy
q: Team members crave a sense of permanence, prideful identity, and belonging.

By highlighting the lasting imprint and enduring contributions left by those who came before, leaders have a powerful tool through which to guide decisions, inspire team members, and create a sense of shared belonging.
Across organizations, common elements of the Legacy include the need for sacrifice, the commitment to work incredibly hard, the quality standards by which people are measured.

Leaders who purposefully create a Legacy, share stories and anecdotes from the past, use rituals and traditions to remind people of the Legacy, offer gifts and tokens that can be passed down to others.
If your enterprise has a history of great accomplishments and heroic actions, consider using them more purposefully to create a Legacy for others to follow.

t: Leaders Who Cant One Day See Themselves Working for Any of Their Team Members
q: As team members develop and grow as contributors and leaders in their own right, they often develop strengths, skills, and experience far above those of the team leader.
Good leaders relish developing and nurturing a team member to such a high level of skill and polish that they get promoted above them.
The very job of leadership is to attract, retain, and develop talent to such a high level as to make the leader superfluous.
If the list is empty, a leader must look in the mirror and ask why.
Self-importance can be debilitating for anyone, but especially for leaders. True learning and leadership require people to suffer an injury to their self-esteem at times.

t: The Problem of Celebrating Short-Term Milestones
q: Celebrating short-term milestones and wins provides immediate motivation, boosts morale, and helps to sustain momentum during longer, challenging projects.
They claim that celebrating too early or at milestones along the journey encourages team members to take their foot off the gas and declare victory prematurely.
While it is certainly possible for people to declare victory too early, it is usually the size and scope of the celebration that sends the wrong message.

The list of possible smaller celebrations is long: an email chain of acknowledgement, recognition on social media, handwritten notes, coffee delivered to workstations, a callout at the end of a meeting.
Leaders who decry celebrating early typically view celebration in a singular dimension of BIG. Small celebrations get the job done, infusing the work with passion and purpose.

t: The Importance of Participation
q: Every teacher wants great participation from their students. But talk to any teacher, and they will tell you that participation is usually patchy.

It is students (not teachers) who need to wrestle with the content, concepts and skills of the curriculum... it is what students are thinking about that will likely determine the success of any lesson.
Put simply, if you're implementing any form of explicit teaching, great rates of student participation are not nice-to-have; they are a must-have.
With such limited evidence of learning, teachers cannot teach responsively because they are flying blind.

The kicker? Students who probably need the most from their teachers -- the most encouragement, the most frequent nods of support, the highest rates of corrective feedback -- are often the very students who give (and receive) the least.
Equitable student participation matters because participation opens doors for more.

t: Coaching Cut #20: The Premortem
q: It's natural to assume our coachee will be motivated to implement their action step, especially as they're often at peak commitment levels during coaching. But when reality sinks in -- marking, meetings, lesson planning etc. --, predictable barriers to implementation get in the way.

A premortem flips that around. You imagine that failure has already happened before your coachee has even attempted to implement the step. This gets ahead of failure by anticipating likely barriers and planning to overcome them before they've even occurred.
By setting up the premortem in this way, Adam can insert himself into the future failure and think more concretely about what might have got him there.
If Sarah had just asked "what might go wrong?", it would have been easier for Adam to fall prey to the optimism bias and not volunteer any likely barriers.

It's way too easy for coach and coachee to assume it's plain sailing after the coaching conversation. But the coaching conversation isn't where most of the learning happens; it just kickstarts the process.
We risk it becoming tokenistic though if we simply end conversations with "what could go wrong?".

t: AI'm Not Doing the Homework
q: Our students are so used to finding things out quickly. Some people say this is a good thing because they've got knowledge at their fingertips. This is incorrect. They have information at their fingertips.
So, without robust foundational knowledge, students will find it difficult to fully comprehend a concept.
They scan the question and the app generates a full step-by-step response to the question. The student then simply copies the answer and they've completed their homework with no thinking involved!

Students have always looked for ways to take shortcuts or avoid the hard work when it comes to homework... Now AI makes it even simpler to bypass the effort, but the challenge of encouraging genuine learning remains the same.
But we cannot assume a poor quiz score in lessons equates a lack of effort with homework.
We must protect the integrity of independent learning and help students engage meaningfully with their work.

t: 3-Read Friday #78: AI Homework, Coaching Premortems, and Participation
q: A few weeks ago, I asked the question: Is Maths homework dead? Homework expert, Jo, delves deeper into the issue, suggesting practical ways we can make homework useful in the age of AI.
A premortem is where you imagine that failure has already happened, analyse why this could have happened, and then take steps to prevent it from happening.
When I watch lessons, I often ask the question: How easy would it be for a student to lack effort or lack understanding, and the teacher be unaware of it?
This is a question of student participation -- something Bronwyn addresses in a trilogy of posts. Here is the first. Read them all.
Sarah shows how this can be a powerful technique when coaching.

t: In Search of Excellence
q: The foundation for the highest competence in any role or skill is aptitude, knowledge, experience, and the drive to learn.
To attain a competence and quality that is extraordinary, a professional must constantly seek feedback, absorb what is actionable, and then incorporate it into their daily execution.
In too many cases, candidates who might be excellent are overlooked because they say the wrong thing or don’t fit the stereotype a leader is looking for.
Those who are highly talented and reach for excellence love to showcase their skills. Those who are just above average or less despise this demonstration.
Surround yourself with excellent people, and pretty soon, learning and feedback spread like wildfire.

t: The Foundational Importance of Executive Functioning
q: Executive Functioning refers to higher-level cognitive skills that allow people to manage their thoughts, actions, and emotions to achieve goals.

The skills that make up Executive Functioning are often described as the “management system of the brain” because they contribute to planning, organizing, concentration, remembering, and the controlling of impulses.
Instead, they have the self-discipline to regulate their behavior to fit the demands of a situation.
Research confirms that Executive Functions develop throughout childhood and adolescence and then remain relatively stable and unchanging throughout adulthood.
In fact, research confirms that much of the professional success people enjoy in life depends largely upon these four elements in the Executive Functioning skill set.

t: Great Leaders Dont Just Select Talent, They Ensemble It
q: But there’s another talent judgment that is equally important and perhaps even more rare—the ability to ensemble talent.
Leaders great at ensembling talent think first about the chemistry and fit between individual talents and skills.
But most of all, they want individuals who will push the buttons that others on the team need to be pushed.
They know it is the unexpected chemistry between qualities (think peanut butter and chocolate) that can make all the difference.
An ensemble of the right stars makes the night sky of any team brighter. Great leaders know how talent fits together.
